They are called neutrinos, the ghost particles. So how do you catch something that passes through a planet? This year, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to one answer: a giant block of ice at the South Pole.

ghost

The story starts in 1930. Wolfgang Pauli saw energy going missing when some atoms decay. As a desperate remedy, he proposed a tiny neutral particle that carries it away, unseen. It took twenty-six years to prove him right. In 1956, Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines caught neutrinos coming from a nuclear reactor.

Why so hard? A neutrino has no electric charge and almost no mass, so it almost never touches the matter it flies through. With a detector the size of a person, you would wait about a hundred years to see one neutrino hit.

Physicists wanted the rarest neutrinos of all: the most energetic ones, from deep space. Space also throws charged particles at us, called cosmic rays. But magnetic fields bend their paths, so we cannot tell where they came from. Neutrinos are made in the same violent places, and nothing bends them. They point straight back home.

In the 1980s, Francis Halzen, a physicist at the University of Wisconsin, had a bold idea. Why build a giant tank of water, when Antarctica already has one, frozen solid? Deep ice is completely dark. No life, very little radioactivity, no earthquakes.

The first test detector, called AMANDA, brought a surprise. The upper ice was full of tiny bubbles that scattered light. But below about fourteen hundred metres, it was astonishingly clear. A flash could travel hundreds of metres.

So how do you put sensors that deep? You do not drill. You melt. A hot water drill, like a giant shower head, melted holes sixty centimetres wide, down to two thousand four hundred and fifty metres. Each hole took about two days.

Then a race against the freeze. Crews lowered a cable of sensors in about eleven hours. Within weeks the water froze solid, locking them in for good. Over seven Antarctic summers, they did this eighty-six times.

But if neutrinos pass through everything, what does the ice see? Very rarely, a neutrino smashes into an atom's nucleus. The crash creates a new charged particle, often a muon, flying on in nearly the same direction.

Now the beautiful part. Inside ice, light slows down, and this particle moves faster than light can move in ice. So it leaves a cone of faint blue light, like the V shaped wake behind a speedboat. This is Cherenkov light.

Which way did it come from? Timing. The cone sweeps through the ice, and sensors light up one after another. Connect the dots in order, and you get a line. Follow it backwards, and it points to a spot in the sky.

On the twenty-second of September 2017, one neutrino arrived with about two hundred and ninety tera electron volts. IceCube sent an alert, and telescopes around the world turned to look. In that direction, a galaxy was flaring: the blazar T X S zero five zero six, about four billion light years away, powered by a giant black hole.
